scenes.heading: Columnar Storage & MPP Architecture
scenes.narration: Two ideas power modern warehouses: storing data by column and processing it across many machines in parallel.

scenes.heading: Row storage vs columnar storage

left.title: Row-oriented
points: Reads every column even if unused

right.title: Columnar
points: Reads only the columns you select

scenes.narration: Row stores keep each record's fields side by side, which is efficient when you fetch one whole row. Columnar layout groups each column's values together, so an analytical query touches only the columns it needs. Similar values also sit next to each other, which makes compression dramatically better.

scenes.heading: Why columnar wins for analytics
bullets: Less I/O: scans skip columns the query never references.
Better compression: uniform column data shrinks 5-10x on disk.
Vectorized execution: engines process column batches at CPU speed.
Cheaper scans: less data read means lower cost and faster answers.
scenes.narration: Because analytics touches few columns but many rows, reading only those columns slashes I/O. Tight compression cuts storage cost and speeds scans further. Together these let engines crunch column batches with vectorized, cache-friendly execution.

scenes.heading: How MPP splits the work
scenes.narration: In massively parallel processing, a coordinator breaks a query into pieces and hands them to many worker nodes. Each node scans its own slice of data at the same time. The partial results are then merged into a single answer, so ten nodes finish roughly ten times faster.

scenes.text: Columnar storage minimizes what you read, and MPP spreads the work so answers arrive fast.
scenes.narration: Columnar storage reduces how much data you touch, and MPP parallelizes the touching, which is why warehouses feel fast at scale.
